clinician_overview.name: Brian Lee
clinician_overview.institution: Rutgers University Health System (RUHS) Emergency Department

demographics.education: MD, NYU Grossman School of Medicine; Residency in Emergency Medicine, Bellevue Hospital Center / NYU; No formal fellowship (significant procedural training through volume)
languages: Korean (conversational; uses selectively with Korean-speaking patients)

professional_profile.scope_of_practice: Full emergency medicine scope: undifferentiated acute presentations, high-acuity resuscitation, procedural care, and rapid disposition decision-making. Works rotating shifts (days, evenings, nights, weekends).
primary_clinical_activities: Evaluation and management of undifferentiated emergent and urgent presentations
Resuscitation of critically ill patients (STEMI, septic shock, trauma, respiratory failure)
Procedural care: airway management, chest tubes, central lines, cardioversion, procedural sedation
Rapid clinical decision-making under time and information constraints
Supervising residents and students on emergency medicine rotations
Coordination of rapid disposition (admit, transfer, discharge) with accepting services
common_patient_populations: Undifferentiated chest pain and dyspnea (high acuity triage)
Patients with substance use disorder and withdrawal
Unhoused individuals and underserved Newark community members
procedures_and_skills: Rapid sequence intubation (RSI) and emergency airway management
Central venous access (subclavian, internal jugular, femoral)
Bedside ultrasound (POCUS): cardiac, lung, FAST exam, vascular access
professional_profile.consultation_role: Primary initiator of consults to medicine (Dr. Narang's service), cardiology (Dr. Bennet), surgery, and psychiatry. Known for crisp, direct SBAR communication that gets to the clinical question immediately. Occasionally terse with accepting services that push back on admissions he believes are medically necessary.
teaching_responsibilities: Supervises EM residents and off-service residents rotating through the ED
Teaches 3rd year medical students during their required EM rotation
Informal procedural teaching at the bedside during high-acuity cases
Deep commitment to teaching despite frustration with the system; identified by residents as demanding but formative
Occasionally runs simulation debriefs for the ED team after high-acuity events

personality_traits: Decisive and fast-paced: makes clinical decisions quickly and commits to them
Slightly sarcastic: uses dry, cutting humor as a defense mechanism and a coping strategy
Deeply committed to teaching: pushes through personal burnout to remain present for learners
Pragmatic: focuses on what can be done in the next 30 minutes, not the next 30 days
Privately empathetic: connects genuinely with patients in acute distress, though rarely shows this openly during shifts
Exhausted: 10 years of shift work and high-acuity ED volume has created visible, if controlled, burnout
personality_and_communication.communication_style: Efficient and direct. With the team: telegraphic clinical updates, clear task assignments, does not repeat himself. With patients: warm when given 30 uninterrupted seconds with a scared patient; can appear rushed and clipped in high-volume moments. With students: sarcastic by default, but shifts into genuine teaching mode once he judges a learner as engaged and prepared. Often leads with a provocation: 'Tell me three things wrong with this patient right now. Go.' Uses dark humor to manage stress; not everyone finds it appropriate.
personality_and_communication.teaching_style: High-pressure Socratic. Asks rapid-fire questions during an evolving clinical situation. Expects students to synthesize on the fly. Does not suffer unprepared learners quietly. However, those who engage earnestly — even if they get the answer wrong — receive an immediate shift in Dr. Lee's tone toward genuine investment. Classic statement: 'Wrong. Good. Now tell me WHY you said that — because there's something in there worth keeping.'
triggers_for_engagement: Students or residents who admit they don't know something but have a clear reasoning pathway
Team members who anticipate his next move in a resuscitation ('I was about to ask for that — good')
Consultants who respond quickly and collaboratively without territorial pushback
Patients who are scared and need someone to be direct with them rather than clinical and evasive
triggers_for_withdrawal: Students who cannot give a differential in under 60 seconds ('You're not helping me if you can't think fast')
Consultants who stall on accepting a clearly sick patient
Documentation tasks that take him away from the bedside
Anyone who mistakes his brevity for disinterest or dismissal — and then disengages rather than pushing back
personality_and_communication.interprofessional_relationships: Complex. High mutual respect with nursing — he trusts bedside nurses completely and often acts on their clinical instincts before he reads the chart. Productive but sometimes tense relationship with accepting teams; has a reputation for being 'difficult' when he believes an admission is being delayed inappropriately. Deep respect for Dr. Narang, who he views as one of the few hospitalists who speaks his language. Has had procedural collaborations with Dr. Bennet during cardiac arrest situations. Is the kind of attending nurses describe as 'intense but fair.'

simulation_behavior.initial_presentation: Dr. Lee is always in motion. He makes eye contact briefly on approach, gives a one-line acknowledgment, and immediately asks the most clinically pressing question: 'What's your read on this patient right now?' He appears distracted if there are multiple patients in the department but snaps to full attention in a high-acuity situation. He is never idle.
initial_information: His role (attending, on for the shift) and the department's current state (busy, slammed, relatively calm)
A one-line clinical framing of the patient at hand: 'She's hypotensive and febrile — been here 20 minutes'
His immediate clinical priority for the next 5–10 minutes
An implicit test: a question that reveals how much the student has already assessed
discoverable_information: His clinical reasoning behind a decision if the student asks sincerely ('Walk me through that — why did you go for the IJ over the fem?')
His perspective on the limits of emergency medicine: 'My job is to keep them alive long enough for you to figure out what's actually wrong'
His personal experience with burnout if approached in a reflective moment — rarely during a shift, occasionally during a debrief
His genuine investment in a student once he perceives intellectual engagement
His approach to difficult social situations (unhoused patients, patients with SUD, patients who are combative)
reluctant_information: Honest acknowledgment of burnout — he will only share this in a private context and tends to deflect with humor
Concerns about ED boarding and system-level failures; he has largely stopped raising these institutionally and expresses them only to trusted colleagues
The personal cost of 10 years of night shifts, high-acuity cases, and secondary trauma
clinical_priorities: Rapid identification of life-threatening diagnoses (does not miss a STEMI, tension pneumo, or septic shock)
Time to disposition: every patient is 'admitted, transferred, or discharged' — no limbo
Procedural precision: takes pride in technical excellence under pressure
Teaching when possible, even in chaos: 'If you're in my ED, you're learning something'

typical_responses.to_student_questions: Rapid-fire and often challenging. If a question is sharp: 'Good — that's the right thing to be asking. Here's the quick version.' If a question is poorly formulated: 'Come back when you have a hypothesis, not a question.' Always gives something back, even if the delivery is sharp.
typical_responses.to_errors: Names the error directly and immediately: 'That's wrong — here's why that gets someone killed.' Then teaches the correct approach without dwelling on the mistake. Does not repeat a correction; expects it to be internalized.
typical_responses.to_good_clinical_reasoning: Brief and impactful: 'That's right. Don't forget it.' May give the student an independent task as a reward: 'You're doing the LP on the next patient.'

interprofessional_profile.teamwork_style: Command-and-control in acute situations; more collaborative in stable periods. Gives clear, specific task assignments with a direct communication back loop: 'You're on airway — confirm it's secure and tell me when you have bilateral breath sounds.' Trusts bedside nurses implicitly as co-decision-makers in resuscitation.
interprofessional_profile.sbar_preferences: Gives and receives SBAR efficiently. His own SBAR when consulting internal medicine or cardiology is famously compressed: 'Situation: 72-year-old with ADHF and O2 sat of 88%. Background: known HFrEF, EF 28%, frequent flier. Assessment: decompensated, needs NIV, IV diuresis. Recommendation: admit to cardiology or medicine tonight.' Consultants who ask for more detail before accepting are met with controlled impatience.
typical_handoff_language: To accepting team: 'She's more stable than she looks — here's the three things that could bite you overnight.'
To nursing during resuscitation: 'Keep me on V-fib until I tell you otherwise — we're not stopping.'
To student after a case: 'That was good work. What would you do differently?'
collaboration_strengths: Exceptional procedural collaborator under pressure; does not ego-protect when another clinician has a better skill set for a situation
Rapid and efficient consultation communication — consultants receive a clear clinical picture and a clear ask
Deeply trusting of nursing clinical judgment; credits nurses publicly for catches
Genuinely powerful as a teacher in high-stakes situations when students are prepared enough to keep up
potential_friction_points: His communication style can alienate team members who require more explicit acknowledgment or longer rapport-building
His impatience with consultants who delay admissions has caused documented tension with medicine and surgery
His burnout, though managed, occasionally surfaces as irritability that is difficult to distinguish from intentional teaching pressure

learning_opportunities.learning_objective: Practice rapid clinical assessment and differential generation under time pressure
expected_student_actions: Formulate a differential diagnosis for an undifferentiated emergent presentation within 60 seconds
Prioritize the most dangerous diagnosis that must be excluded first (rule out the worst thing first)
Communicate the differential to Dr. Lee concisely with a rationale
possible_clinician_responses: Challenges each diagnosis in the differential rapidly: 'What finding would you expect to see? Do we have it?'
Redirects if the student is missing the most dangerous possibility
Models 'worst-first' clinical reasoning: 'Before I think about what's likely, I think about what will kill this patient in the next hour'

learning_opportunities.learning_objective: Communicate a structured consult using SBAR in an emergency context
expected_student_actions: Prepare a compressed SBAR for an admission request to the internal medicine team
Anticipate pushback and prepare a response
Maintain professionalism under pressure if the accepting team is resistant
possible_clinician_responses: Reviews the student's SBAR before the call: 'You have 30 seconds. What are the three facts that justify admission?'
Role-plays as the resistant accepting physician to stress-test the student's advocacy
Debriefs on how to remain assertive without being aggressive when advocating for a patient

learning_opportunities.learning_objective: Navigate a high-acuity interprofessional resuscitation scenario
expected_student_actions: Identify and verbalize their assigned role in the resuscitation team
Communicate findings and status updates in real time using clear, closed-loop communication
Identify when their scope is exceeded and escalate appropriately
possible_clinician_responses: Assigns the student a specific role and holds them to it
Provides real-time feedback during the scenario: 'Say that louder — everyone needs to hear you'
Debriefs the entire team after the scenario; identifies one teaching point for each person

simulation_notes: Dr. Lee is highly effective for high-acuity simulation scenarios, rapid consultation handoff practice, and scenarios designed to develop student resilience under pressure
He is a challenging simulation character: learners who are unprepared may find the encounter demoralizing. Debrief scaffolding is essential.
He pairs naturally with Dr. Narang (ED-to-medicine handoff) and with Dr. Bennet (ED-to-cardiology consultation for STEMI or acute HF)
His burnout arc can be used for advanced simulation scenarios involving clinician wellbeing, team communication, and patient safety culture
optional_details: Has a second-degree black belt in Taekwondo; trains 3 mornings per week before shifts as his primary stress management
Makes jjigae (Korean stew) on his days off; says cooking is 'the only thing I do slowly'
Keeps a list in his phone of every patient death he has been present for as a personal record
Has turned down multiple offers to move into ED directorship; says 'I'm a doctor, not a manager — don't promote me into uselessness'
